metadata.title: Necessary Conditions for Tractability of Valued CSPs

nodes.name: relation (m-ary relation over $D$)
nodes.statement: An $m$-ary \emph{relation} over $D$ is any mapping $\phi:D^m\to\{c,\infty\}$ for some $c\in\mathbb{Q}$. We denote by $\rel_D^{(m)}$ the set of all $m$-ary relations and let $\rel_D=\bigcup_{m\geq 1}{\rel_D^{(m)}}$.

nodes.name: weighted relation
nodes.statement: An $m$-ary \emph{weighted relation}\footnote{In some paper weighted relations are called cost functions.} over $D$ is any mapping $\phi:D^m\to\qq$. We denote by $\wrel_D^{(m)}$ the set of all $m$-ary weighted relations and let $\wrel_D=\bigcup_{m\ge 1}{\wrel_D^{(m)}}$.

nodes.name: feasibility relation $\feas(\phi)$
nodes.statement: For any $m$-ary weighted relation $\phi\in\wrel_D^{(m)}$, we denote by $\feas(\phi)=\{\tup{x}\in D^m\:|\:\phi(\tup{x})<\infty\}\in\rel_D^{(m)}$ the underlying \emph{feasibility relation}.

nodes.name: finite-valued weighted relation
nodes.statement: A weighted relation $\phi:D^m\to\qq$ is called \emph{finite-valued} if $\feas(\phi)=D^m$.

nodes.name: valued constraint
nodes.statement: Let $V=\{x_1,\ldots, x_n\}$ be a set of variables. A \emph{valued constraint} over $V$ is an expression of the form $\phi(\tup{x})$ where $\phi\in \wrel_D^{(m)}$ and $\tup{x}\in V^m$. The number $m$ is called the \emph{arity} of the constraint, the weighted relation $\phi$ is called the \emph{constraint weighted relation}, and the tuple $\tup{x}$ the \emph{scope} of the constraint.

nodes.name: valued constraint language
nodes.statement: Any set $\Gamma\subseteq\wrel_D$ is called a \emph{valued constraint language}\footnote{A valued constraint language $\Gamma$ is sometimes called \emph{general-valued} to emphasise the fact that weighted relations from $\Gamma$ are not necessarily finite-valued.} over $D$, or simply a \emph{language}. We will denote by $\VCSP(\Gamma)$ the class of all VCSP instances in which the constraint weighted relations are all contained in $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: tractable / intractable valued constraint language
nodes.statement: A valued constraint language $\Gamma$ is called \emph{tractable} if $\VCSP(\Gamma')$ can be solved (to optimality) in polynomial time for every finite subset $\Gamma'\subseteq\Gamma$, and $\Gamma$ is called \emph{intractable} if $\VCSP(\Gamma')$ is NP-hard for some finite $\Gamma'\subseteq\Gamma$.
differentia: $\VCSP(\Gamma')$ can be solved (to optimality) in polynomial time for every finite subset $\Gamma'\subseteq\Gamma$

nodes.name: finite-valued constraint language
nodes.statement: A valued constraint language is called \emph{finite-valued} if every weighted relation $\phi$ from the language is finite-valued.
differentia: every weighted relation $\phi$ from the language is finite-valued

nodes.name: $\feas(\Gamma)$
nodes.statement: We denote by $\feas(\Gamma)=\{\dom(\phi)\:|\:\phi\in\Gamma\}$ the set of underlying relations of all weighted relations from $\Gamma$.
nodes.genus: the set of underlying relations of all weighted relations from $\Gamma$

nodes.name: expressible weighted relation
nodes.statement: We say that an $m$-ary weighted relation $\phi$ is \emph{expressible} over a valued constraint language $\Gamma$ if there exists a VCSP instance $\inst \in \VCSP(\Gamma)$ with variables $V=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_m\}$, such that \begin{equation} \phi(y_1,\ldots,y_m) = \min_{x_1\in D,\ldots,x_n\in D}\inst(x_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_m)\,. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\phi$ is expressible over $\Gamma$ if it arises by minimising a $\VCSP(\Gamma)$ instance over auxiliary variables.
differentia: there exists a VCSP instance $\inst \in \VCSP(\Gamma)$ with variables $V=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_m\}$, such that $\phi(y_1,\ldots,y_m) = \min_{x_1\in D,\ldots,x_n\in D}\inst(x_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_m)$

nodes.name: closed under expressibility
nodes.statement: A valued constraint language $\Gamma$ is \emph{closed under expressibility} if every weighted relation $\phi$ expressible over $\Gamma$ belongs to $\Gamma$.
differentia: every weighted relation $\phi$ expressible over $\Gamma$ belongs to $\Gamma$

nodes.name: weighted relational clone
nodes.statement: A valued constraint language $\Gamma \subseteq \wrel_D$ is called a \emph{weighted relational clone} if it contains the binary equality relation $\phi_=$ on $D$ and is closed under expressibility, scaling by non-negative rational constants (where we define $0\cdot\infty=\infty$), and addition of rational constants. For any $\Gamma$, we define $\wrelclone(\Gamma)$ to be the smallest weighted relational clone containing $\Gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: A valued constraint language containing $\phi_=$ and closed under expressibility, nonnegative scaling and addition of constants.
differentia: it contains the binary equality relation $\phi_=$ on $D$
scaling by non-negative rational constants (where we define $0\cdot\infty=\infty$)

nodes.name: relational clone
nodes.statement: A \emph{relational clone} is a weighted relational clone containing only (unweighted) relations.\footnote{Equivalently, a set of relations containing the binary equality relation and closed under conjunction and existential quantification.} For a set of relations $\Gamma$, we denote by $\relclone(\Gamma)$ the smallest relational clone containing $\Gamma$.

nodes.name: polymorphism
nodes.statement: Let $\phi$ be an $m$-ary weighted relation on $D$ and let $f$ be a $k$-ary operation on $D$. Then $f$ is a \emph{polymorphism} of $\phi$ if, for any $\tup{x_1},\tup{x_2},\ldots,\tup{x_k} \in D^m$ with $\tup{x_i}\in\dom(\phi)$ for all $1\leq i\leq k$, we have that $f(\tup{x_1},\tup{x_2},\ldots,\tup{x_k})\in\dom(\phi)$. For any valued constraint language $\Gamma$ over a set $D$, we denote by $\pol(\Gamma)$ the set of all operations on $D$ which are polymorphisms of all $\phi \in \Gamma$. We write $\pol(\phi)$ for $\pol(\{\phi\})$.
nodes.statement_short: $f$ is a polymorphism of $\phi$ if it maps feasible tuples of $\phi$ to feasible tuples.
differentia: for any $\tup{x_1},\tup{x_2},\ldots,\tup{x_k} \in D^m$ with $\tup{x_i}\in\dom(\phi)$ for all $1\leq i\leq k$, we have that $f(\tup{x_1},\tup{x_2},\ldots,\tup{x_k})\in\dom(\phi)$

nodes.name: projection $\proj^{(k)}_i$
nodes.statement: A $k$-ary \emph{projection} is an operation of the form $\proj^{(k)}_i(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=x_i$ for some $1\leq i\leq k$.
differentia: of the form $\proj^{(k)}_i(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=x_i$ for some $1\leq i\leq k$

nodes.name: superposition of operations
nodes.statement: The \emph{superposition} of a $k$-ary operation $f:D^k\rightarrow D$ with $k$ $\ell$-ary operations $g_i:D^\ell\rightarrow D$ for $1\leq i\leq k$ is the $\ell$-ary function $f[g_1,\ldots,g_k]:D^\ell\to D$ defined by \begin{equation} f[g_1,\ldots,g_k](x_1,\ldots,x_\ell)=f(g_1(x_1,\ldots,x_\ell),\ldots,g_k(x_1,\ldots,x_\ell))\,. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Composition of an operation with a tuple of operations of equal arity.

nodes.name: clone of operations
nodes.statement: A \emph{clone} of operations, $C$, is a set of operations on $D$ that contains all projections and is closed under superposition. The $k$-ary operations in a clone $C$ will be denoted by $C^{(k)}$.

nodes.name: weighting of a clone
nodes.statement: A $k$-ary \emph{weighting} of a clone $C$ is a function $\omega : C^{(k)} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q}$ such that $\omega(f) < 0$ only if $f$ is a projection and \begin{equation} \sum_{f \in C^{(k)}}\omega(f)\ =\ 0\,. \end{equation} We define $\supp(\omega)=\{f\in C^{(k)}\:|\:\omega(f)>0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: A rational weight function on $C^{(k)}$ summing to $0$, negative only on projections.

nodes.name: superposition of a weighting; proper superposition
nodes.statement: For any clone $C$, any $k$-ary weighting $\omega$ of $C$, and any $g_1,\ldots,g_k \in C^{(\ell)}$, the \emph{superposition} of $\omega$ and $g_1,\ldots,g_k$, is the function $\omega[g_1,\ldots,g_k]: C^{(\ell)} \rightarrow \mathbb{Q}$ defined by \begin{equation} \omega[g_1,\ldots,g_k](f') = \sum_{\{f \in C^{(k)}\:|\:f[g_1,\ldots,g_k] = f'\}}\omega(f)\,. \end{equation} If $\omega$ satisfies~\eqref{ineq:weightingzero} then so does $\omega[g_1,\ldots,g_k]$. If the result of a superposition is a valid weighting (that is, negative weights are only assigned to projections) then that superposition will be called a \emph{proper} superposition.
nodes.statement_short: Push a weighting forward along a tuple of operations; the superposition is proper when the result is again a weighting.

nodes.name: weighted clone
nodes.statement: A \emph{weighted clone}, $W$, is a non-empty set of weightings of some fixed clone $C$, called the \emph{support clone} of $W$, which is closed under nonnegative scaling, addition of weightings of equal arity, and proper superposition with operations from $C$. We define $\supp(W)=\bigcup_{\omega\in W}\supp(\omega)$.
nodes.statement_short: A nonempty set of weightings of a fixed support clone, closed under nonnegative scaling, addition and proper superposition.
nodes.genus: non-empty set of weightings of some fixed clone $C$
differentia: addition of weightings of equal arity

nodes.name: weighted polymorphism
nodes.statement: Let $\phi$ be an $m$-ary weighted relation on $D$ and let $\omega$ be a $k$-ary weighting of a clone $C$ of operations on $D$. We call $\omega$ a \emph{weighted polymorphism} of $\phi$ if $C\subseteq\pol(\phi)$ and for any $\tup{x}_1,\tup{x}_2,\ldots,\tup{x}_k \in D^m$ with $\tup{x}_i\in\dom(\phi)$ for all $1\leq i\leq k$, we have \begin{equation} \sum_{f \in C^{(k)}}\omega(f)\phi(f(\tup{x}_1,\tup{x}_2,\ldots,\tup{x}_k)) \ \leq\ 0\,. \end{equation} If $\omega$ is a weighted polymorphism of $\phi$ we say that $\phi$ is \emph{improved} by $\omega$.
nodes.statement_short: $\omega$ improves $\phi$ when the $\omega$-weighted sum of $\phi$-values over superposed feasible tuples is nonpositive.
differentia: for any $\tup{x}_1,\tup{x}_2,\ldots,\tup{x}_k \in D^m$ with $\tup{x}_i\in\dom(\phi)$ for all $1\leq i\leq k$, we have $\sum_{f \in C^{(k)}}\omega(f)\phi(f(\tup{x}_1,\tup{x}_2,\ldots,\tup{x}_k)) \ \leq\ 0$

nodes.name: $\wpol(\Gamma)$
nodes.statement: For any $\Gamma \subseteq \wrel_D$, we define $\wpol(\Gamma)$ to be the set of all weightings of $\pol(\Gamma)$ which are weighted polymorphisms of all weighted relations $\phi \in \Gamma$. We write $\wpol(\phi)$ for $\wpol(\{\phi\})$.
differentia: which are weighted polymorphisms of all weighted relations $\phi \in \Gamma$

nodes.name: $\wops_D$
nodes.statement: We define $\wops_D$ to be the union of the sets $\wops_C$ over all clones $C$ on $D$.

nodes.name: $\wclone(W)$
nodes.statement: We define $\wclone(W)$ to be the smallest weighted clone containing this set of extended weightings obtained from $W$.

nodes.name: $\imp(W)$
nodes.statement: For any $W \subseteq \wops_D$, we denote by $\imp(W)$ the set of all weighted relations in $\wrel_D$ which are improved by all weightings $\omega \in W$.
nodes.genus: set of all weighted relations in $\wrel_D$
differentia: which are improved by all weightings $\omega \in W$

nodes.name: tractable / intractable weighted clone
nodes.statement: A weighted clone $W$ is called \emph{tractable} if $\imp(W)$ is tractable, and intractable if $\imp(W)$ is intractable.

nodes.name: positive weighting
nodes.statement: A weighting is called \emph{positive} if it assigns positive weight to at least one operation that is not a projection.
differentia: it assigns positive weight to at least one operation that is not a projection

nodes.name: sharp operation
nodes.statement: For any $k\geq 2$, a $k$-ary operation $f$ is called \emph{sharp} if $f$ is not a projection, but the operation obtained by equating any two inputs in $f$ is a projection~\cite{Csakany05:minimal}. All sharp operations must satisfy the identity $f(x,x,\ldots,x) = x$; such operations are called \emph{idempotent}.
differentia: the operation obtained by equating any two inputs in $f$ is a projection

nodes.name: majority operation
nodes.statement: The first column in Table~\ref{tab:sharp3} corresponds to operations that satisfy the identities $f(x,x,y)=f(x,y,x)=f(y,x,x)=x$ for all $x,y\in D$; such operations are called \emph{majority} operations.
differentia: satisfy the identities $f(x,x,y)=f(x,y,x)=f(y,x,x)=x$ for all $x,y\in D$

nodes.name: minority operation
nodes.statement: The last column in the table corresponds to operations that satisfy the identities $f(x,x,y)=f(x,y,x)=f(y,x,x)=y$ for all $x,y\in D$; such operations are called \emph{minority} operations.
differentia: satisfy the identities $f(x,x,y)=f(x,y,x)=f(y,x,x)=y$ for all $x,y\in D$

nodes.name: Pixley operation
nodes.statement: Columns 5, 6, and 7 in Table~\ref{tab:sharp3} correspond to operations that satisfy the identities $f(y,y,x) = f(x,y,x) = f(y,x,x)=y$ for all $x,y \in D$ (up to permutations of inputs); such operations are called \emph{Pixley} operations~\cite{Csakany05:minimal}.
differentia: satisfy the identities $f(y,y,x) = f(x,y,x) = f(y,x,x)=y$ for all $x,y \in D$ (up to permutations of inputs)

nodes.name: semiprojection
nodes.statement: For any $k \geq 3$, a $k$-ary operation $f$ is called a \emph{semiprojection} if it is not a projection, but there is an index $1\leq i \leq k$ such that $f(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=\proj^{(k)}_i$ for all $x_1,\ldots,x_k\in D$ such that $x_1,\ldots,x_k$ are not pairwise distinct. In other words, a semiprojection is a particular form of sharp operation where the operation obtained by equating any two inputs is always the \emph{same} projection. Columns 2, 3, and 4 in Table~\ref{tab:sharp3} correspond to semiprojections.
nodes.statement_short: A sharp operation for which identifying any two inputs always yields the same projection.
differentia: there is an index $1\leq i \leq k$ such that $f(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=\proj^{(k)}_i$ for all $x_1,\ldots,x_k\in D$ such that $x_1,\ldots,x_k$ are not pairwise distinct

nodes.name: cyclic permutations $\perm_k$ and $f^\pi$
nodes.statement: We denote by $\perm_k$ the set of $k$ cyclic permutations on $\{1,\ldots,k\}$. We denote by $\circ$ the composition of two permutations, that is, for any $\sigma,\pi\in\perm_k$ we have $\sigma\circ\pi\in\perm_k$ is defined by $\sigma\circ\pi(x)=\sigma(\pi(x))$. For a $k$-ary operation $f$ and a permutation $\pi\in\perm_k$ we will denote by $f^\pi$ the operation $f^\pi=f[\proj^{(k)}_{\pi(1)},\ldots,\proj^{(k)}_{\pi(k)}]$, that is, $f^\pi(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=f(x_{\pi(1)},\ldots,x_{\pi(k)})$.
nodes.statement_short: Notation for cyclic permutations and the argument-permuted operation $f^\pi$.

nodes.name: core (weighted clone / valued constraint language)
nodes.statement: A weighted clone $W$ is a \emph{core} if for every unary weighting $\omega\in W$ every operation $f\in\supp(\omega)$ is bijective. A valued constraint language $\Gamma$ is a core if $W=\wpol(\Gamma)$ is a core.
differentia: for every unary weighting $\omega\in W$ every operation $f\in\supp(\omega)$ is bijective

nodes.name: rigid core
nodes.statement: A weighted clone $W$ is a \emph{rigid core} if the only unary operation in the support clone of $W$ is the unary projection $\proj^{(1)}_1$. A valued constraint language $\Gamma$ is a rigid core if $W=\wpol(\Gamma)$ is a rigid core; that is if the only unary polymorphism of $\Gamma$ is $\proj^{(1)}_1$.
differentia: the only unary operation in the support clone of $W$ is the unary projection $\proj^{(1)}_1$

nodes.name: crisp weighted relational clone / crisp weighted clone
nodes.statement: A weighted relational clone that contains only relations (and thus is a relational clone) is called \emph{crisp}. A weighted clone $W$ is called crisp if $\imp(W)$ is a crisp weighted relational clone.
differentia: contains only relations (and thus is a relational clone)

nodes.name: near-unanimity operation
nodes.statement: A $k$-ary operation $f:D^k\to D$, where $k\geq 3$, is called a \emph{near-unanimity} operation if for all $x,y\in D$, \begin{equation} f(y,x,x,\ldots,x)=f(x,y,x,x,\ldots,x)=\cdots=f(x,x,\ldots,x,y)=x\,. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: An operation returning the repeated argument whenever all but one input coincide.

nodes.name: conservative, commutative and tournament operations
nodes.statement: A binary operation $f:D^2\rightarrow D$ is called conservative if $f(x,y)\in\{x,y\}$ for all $x,y\in D$ and commutative if $f(x,y)=f(y,x)$ for all $x,y\in D$. Moreover, $f$ is called a \emph{tournament} operation if $f$ is both conservative and commutative.

nodes.name: rectangular band
nodes.statement: In fact, $f$ is an example of a \emph{rectangular band}~\cite{McKenzie87:algebras}, which is an idempotent and associative binary operation $f:D^2\to D$ satisfying $f(x,f(y,z))=f(x,z)$ for all $x,y,z\in D$.
nodes.genus: idempotent and associative binary operation $f:D^2\to D$

nodes.name: multimorphism
nodes.statement: A $k$-ary weighting $\omega$ is a \emph{multimorphism} if $\omega(f)\in\mathbb{N}$ for all $f\in\supp(\omega)$ and $\omega(\proj^{(k)}_i)=-1$ for all $1\leq i\leq k$~\cite{Cohen06:complexitysoft}.

nodes.name: $\inv(C)$
nodes.statement: we denote, for a clone $C$, by $\inv(C)$ the relational clone that consists of relations $R$ with $f\in\pol(R)$ for every $f\in C$.
differentia: consists of relations $R$ with $f\in\pol(R)$ for every $f\in C$

nodes.name: finite-valued weighted clone
nodes.statement: A weighted clone $W$ on $D$ is called \emph{finite-valued} if the support clone of $W$ is $\mathbf{I}_D$.

nodes.name: unary constant relation $\phi_d$ and $\mathcal{R}$
nodes.statement: For any $d\in D$, the unary constant relation $\phi_d$ is defined by $\phi_d(x)=0$ if $x=d$ and $\phi_d(x)=\infty$ otherwise. Let $\mathcal{R}=\relclone(\{\phi_=\}\cup\cup_{d\in D}\{\phi_d\})$.

nodes.name: trivial relation
nodes.statement: An $m$-ary relation $R$ on $D$ is called trivial if $R=D^m$.

nodes.name: maximal weighted relational clone
nodes.statement: A weighted relational clone $\Gamma\subseteq\wrel_D$ is called \emph{maximal} if $\wrelclone(\Gamma)\neq\wrel_D$ but for any $\phi\not\in\Gamma$ we have $\wrelclone(\Gamma\cup\{\phi\})=\wrel_D$.

nodes.name: minimal weighted clone
nodes.statement: A weighted clone $W$ with support clone $C$ is called \emph{minimal} if $W\neq\wops_C^0$ and every positive weighting $\omega\in W$ satisfies $\wclone(\omega)=W$.

nodes.name: type of a Pixley operation / semiprojection
nodes.statement: We call (ternary) operations corresponding to columns 5, 6, and 7 in Table~\ref{tab:sharp3} Pixley operations of type 1, 2, and 3 respectively, and will denote by P1 (P2 and P3) the Pixley operations of type 1 (2 and 3, respectively). We call (ternary) semiprojections corresponding to columns 2, 3, and 4 in Table~\ref{tab:sharp3} semiprojections of type 1, 2, and 3 respectively, and will denote by S1 (S2 and S3) the semiprojections of type 1 (2 and 3, respectively). More generally, a $k$-ary semiprojection $f$ is called of type $1\leq i\leq k$ if equating any two inputs of $f$ results in $\proj^{(k)}_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Types 1-3 label Pixley operations and ternary semiprojections by which projection input-identification produces.

nodes.name: related operations
nodes.statement: Two Pixley operations $f$ and $g$ of different types are called \emph{related} if there is a permutation $\pi\in\perm_3$ such that $f=g^\pi$. (Note that the requirement of $f$ and $g$ being of different types excludes the identity permutation $(1,2,3)$ and there are only other two permutations in $\perm_3$, namely $(2,3,1)$ and $(3,1,2)$.) Similarly, two semiprojections $f$ and $g$ of different types are called related if there is a permutation $\pi\in\perm_3$ such that $f=g^\pi$.
nodes.genus: Two Pixley operations $f$ and $g$ of different types
differentia: there is a permutation $\pi\in\perm_3$ such that $f=g^\pi$

nodes.name: cyclic operation / cyclic weighting
nodes.statement: A $k$-ary operation if \emph{cyclic} if $f(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_k)=f(x_2,\ldots,x_k,x_1)$ for every $x_1,\ldots,x_k$. A weighting $\omega$ is cyclic if every operation $f\in\supp(\omega)$ is cyclic.

nodes.name: Theorem 1 (Galois connection between weighted relational clones and weighted clones)
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item For any finite $D$ and any finite $\Gamma \subseteq \wrel_D$, $\imp(\wpol(\Gamma)) = \wrelclone(\Gamma)$. \item For any finite $D$ and any finite $W\subseteq \wops_D$, $\wpol(\imp(W)) = \wclone(W)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: One-to-one Galois correspondence between weighted relational clones and weighted clones.
assumptions: For any finite $D$ and any finite $\Gamma \subseteq \wrel_D$
For any finite $D$ and any finite $W\subseteq \wops_D$

nodes.name: Theorem 2 (reduction to core valued constraint languages)
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a valued constraint language on $D$. If $\Gamma$ is not a core then there is a core valued constraint language $\Gamma'$ on $D'\subseteq D$ such that $\Gamma$ is tractable if and only if $\Gamma'$ is tractable and $\Gamma$ is intractable if and only if $\Gamma'$ is intractable.
nodes.statement_short: Every non-core valued constraint language can be replaced by a complexity-equivalent core on a smaller domain.
assumptions: Let $\Gamma$ be a valued constraint language on $D$
If $\Gamma$ is not a core
conclusions: there is a core valued constraint language $\Gamma'$ on $D'\subseteq D$ such that $\Gamma$ is tractable if and only if $\Gamma'$ is tractable and $\Gamma$ is intractable if and only if $\Gamma'$ is intractable

nodes.name: Theorem 3 (reduction to rigid core valued constraint languages)
nodes.statement: Let $\Gamma$ be a valued constraint language on $D$. If $\Gamma$ is not a rigid core then there is a rigid core valued constraint language $\Gamma'$ on $D'\subseteq D$ such that $\Gamma$ is tractable if and only if $\Gamma'$ is tractable and $\Gamma$ is intractable and only if $\Gamma'$ is intractable.
nodes.statement_short: Restricting to rigid cores does not change tractability.
assumptions: Let $\Gamma$ be a valued constraint language on $D$
If $\Gamma$ is not a rigid core
conclusions: there is a rigid core valued constraint language $\Gamma'$ on $D'\subseteq D$ such that $\Gamma$ is tractable if and only if $\Gamma'$ is tractable and $\Gamma$ is intractable and only if $\Gamma'$ is intractable

nodes.name: Theorem 4 (Creed & Zivny classification of supports of positive weightings)
nodes.statement: Any weighted clone $W$ containing a positive weighting contains a weighting whose support is either: \begin{enumerate} \item a set of unary operations that are not projections; or \item a set of binary idempotent operations that are not projections; or \item a set of ternary operations that are majority operations, minority operations, Pixley operations or semiprojections; or \item a set of $k$-ary semiprojections (for some $k > 3$). \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Four possible support types for some weighting inside any weighted clone with a positive weighting.
nodes.origin_citation: Creed & Zivny 2011 (Theorem 2); see also Cohen et al. 2013 (Corollary 7.7)
assumptions: Any weighted clone $W$ containing a positive weighting
conclusions: contains a weighting whose support is either: a set of unary operations that are not projections; or a set of binary idempotent operations that are not projections; or a set of ternary operations that are majority operations, minority operations, Pixley operations or semiprojections; or a set of $k$-ary semiprojections (for some $k > 3$)

nodes.name: Theorem 5 (Main)
nodes.statement: Any weighted clone $W$ that is a rigid core and contains a positive weighting also contains a weighting whose support is either: \begin{enumerate} \item a set of binary idempotent operations that are not projections; or \item a set of ternary operations that are either: \begin{enumerate} \item a set of majority operations; or \item a set of minority operations; or \item a set of majority operations with total weight $2$ and a set of minority operations with total weight $1$; or \end{enumerate} \item a set of $k$-ary semiprojections (for some $k \geq 3$). \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Refines Theorem 4 for rigid cores: Pixley operations are eliminated and the ternary case splits into pure majority, pure minority, or weight-2/weight-1 majority-minority mixtures.
assumptions: Any weighted clone $W$ that is a rigid core and contains a positive weighting
conclusions: also contains a weighting whose support is either: a set of binary idempotent operations that are not projections; or a set of ternary operations that are either: a set of majority operations; or a set of minority operations; or a set of majority operations with total weight $2$ and a set of minority operations with total weight $1$; or a set of $k$-ary semiprojections (for some $k \geq 3$)

nodes.name: Theorem 9 (a majority operation in some support implies tractability)
nodes.statement: Let $W$ be a weighted clone. If there is a weighting $\omega\in W$ such that $\supp(\omega)$ contains a majority operation then $W$ is tractable.
assumptions: Let $W$ be a weighted clone
If there is a weighting $\omega\in W$ such that $\supp(\omega)$ contains a majority operation

nodes.name: Theorem 11 (maximal non-crisp weighted relational clones are intractable)
nodes.statement: All maximal non-crisp weighted relational clones are intractable.
assumptions: All maximal non-crisp weighted relational clones

nodes.name: Gordan's Theorem
nodes.statement: Let $A\in\mathbb{Q}^{n\times m}$ be a matrix. Either $Ax=0$, where $x\in\mathbb{Q}^{m}$ with $x\geq 0$ and $x\neq 0$, or $\exists y\in\mathbb{Q}^n$ with $y^{\intercal}A>0$.
nodes.statement_short: LP-duality alternative: either a nonzero nonnegative kernel vector exists, or a strictly positive row combination does.
assumptions: Let $A\in\mathbb{Q}^{n\times m}$ be a matrix
conclusions: Either $Ax=0$, where $x\in\mathbb{Q}^{m}$ with $x\geq 0$ and $x\neq 0$, or $\exists y\in\mathbb{Q}^n$ with $y^{\intercal}A>0$

nodes.name: Świerczkowski's Lemma
nodes.statement: The only sharp operations of arity $k\geq 4$ are semiprojections.
assumptions: sharp operations of arity $k\geq 4$

nodes.name: Lemma 2 (symmetrisation of a positive weighting)
nodes.statement: Let $W$ be a weighted clone and $\omega\in W$ a positive $k$-ary weighting. Then there is a positive $k$-ary weighting $\mu\in W$ with the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item $\displaystyle\supp(\mu)=\bigcup_{f\in\supp(\omega)}\bigcup_{\pi\in\perm_k} f^\pi$; \item $\mu(\proj^{(k)}_i)=-1$ for every $1\leq i\leq k$; \item $\mu(f)=\mu(f^\pi)$ for every $f\in\supp(\mu)$ and $\pi\in\perm_k$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Any positive weighting can be symmetrised over cyclic permutations and normalised so each projection gets weight $-1$.
assumptions: Let $W$ be a weighted clone and $\omega\in W$ a positive $k$-ary weighting
conclusions: there is a positive $k$-ary weighting $\mu\in W$ with the following properties: $\displaystyle\supp(\mu)=\bigcup_{f\in\supp(\omega)}\bigcup_{\pi\in\perm_k} f^\pi$; $\mu(\proj^{(k)}_i)=-1$ for every $1\leq i\leq k$; $\mu(f)=\mu(f^\pi)$ for every $f\in\supp(\mu)$ and $\pi\in\perm_k$

nodes.name: Lemma 3 (weighted sums of superpositions)
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a clone, and let $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ be weightings of $C$, of arity $k$ and $\ell$ respectively. For any $g_1,\ldots,g_k \in C^{(m)}$ and any $g'_1,\ldots,g'_\ell \in C^{(m)}$, \begin{equation*} c_1 \, \omega_1[g_1,\ldots,g_k] + \ c_2 \, \omega_2[g'_1,\ldots,g'_{\ell}] = \omega[g_1,\ldots,g_k,g'_1,\ldots,g'_{\ell}]\,, \end{equation*} where $\omega = c_1 \, \omega_1[e^{(k+\ell)}_1,\ldots,e^{(k+\ell)}_k] + \ c_2 \, \omega_2[e^{(k+\ell)}_{k+1},\ldots,e^{(k+\ell)}_{k+\ell}]$
nodes.statement_short: A weighted sum of two superpositions equals a single superposition of a weighted sum of projection-superpositions, so improper intermediate steps are harmless.
nodes.origin_citation: Cohen, Cooper, Creed, Jeavons & Zivny 2013, Lemma 6.4
assumptions: Let $C$ be a clone, and let $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ be weightings of $C$, of arity $k$ and $\ell$ respectively
For any $g_1,\ldots,g_k \in C^{(m)}$ and any $g'_1,\ldots,g'_\ell \in C^{(m)}$

nodes.name: Cohen et al. Lemma 6.23 (criterion for expressibility as a sum of unary weighted relations)
nodes.statement: We will use~\cite[Lemma~6.23]{Cohen06:complexitysoft} which says that a weighted relation $\phi:D^m\to\Q$ can be expressed as a sum of unary weighted relations if and only if, for all $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in D^m$ and all $1\leq i\leq m$, we have \begin{equation} \phi(\tup{x})+\phi(\tup{y}) = \phi(\tup{x}[i\leftarrow \tup{y}[i]]) + \phi(\tup{y}[i\leftarrow \tup{x}[i]])\,. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: A weighted relation decomposes into unary terms exactly when swapping any single coordinate preserves the sum of values.
assumptions: a weighted relation $\phi:D^m\to\Q$
conclusions: can be expressed as a sum of unary weighted relations if and only if, for all $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in D^m$ and all $1\leq i\leq m$, we have $\phi(\tup{x})+\phi(\tup{y}) = \phi(\tup{x}[i\leftarrow \tup{y}[i]]) + \phi(\tup{y}[i\leftarrow \tup{x}[i]])$

nodes.name: Proposition 6 (majority weighting implies crisp)
nodes.statement: Let $W$ be a weighted clone with a positive ternary weighting $\omega\in W$ such that all operations $f\in\supp(\omega)$ are majority operations. Then $W$ is crisp.
assumptions: Let $W$ be a weighted clone with a positive ternary weighting $\omega\in W$ such that all operations $f\in\supp(\omega)$ are majority operations

nodes.name: Proposition 7 (near-unanimity weighting implies crisp)
nodes.statement: Let $W$ be a weighted clone with a positive weighting $\omega\in W$ such that all operations $f\in\supp(\omega)$ are near-unanimity operations. Then $W$ is crisp.
assumptions: Let $W$ be a weighted clone with a positive weighting $\omega\in W$ such that all operations $f\in\supp(\omega)$ are near-unanimity operations

nodes.name: Proposition 8 (minority weighting implies crisp)
nodes.statement: Let $W$ be a weighted clone with a positive ternary weighting $\omega\in W$ such that all operations $f\in\supp(\omega)$ are minority operations. Then $W$ is crisp.
assumptions: Let $W$ be a weighted clone with a positive ternary weighting $\omega\in W$ such that all operations $f\in\supp(\omega)$ are minority operations

nodes.name: Proposition 10 (finite-valued case of Theorem 5 (2c))
nodes.statement: Let $W$ be a finite-valued weighted clone. If $W$ contains a positive weighting described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(2c) then every weighted relation $\phi\in\imp(W)$ can be expressed as a sum of unary weighted relations and the binary equality relation $\phi_=$.
nodes.statement_short: In the finite-valued case a majority/minority mixed weighting forces every improved weighted relation to decompose into unary terms plus equality.
assumptions: Let $W$ be a finite-valued weighted clone
If $W$ contains a positive weighting described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(2c)
conclusions: every weighted relation $\phi\in\imp(W)$ can be expressed as a sum of unary weighted relations and the binary equality relation $\phi_=$

nodes.name: Tractability transfers to the generated weighted relational clone
nodes.statement: It has been shown that $\Gamma$ is tractable if and only if $\wrelclone(\Gamma)$ is tractable~\cite{cccjz13:sicomp}. Consequently, when trying to identify tractable valued constraint languages, it is sufficient to consider only weighted relational clones.
nodes.statement_short: $\Gamma$ and $\wrelclone(\Gamma)$ have the same tractability status.
assumptions: $\Gamma$
conclusions: $\Gamma$ is tractable if and only if $\wrelclone(\Gamma)$ is tractable

nodes.name: $\pol(\Gamma)$ is a clone
nodes.statement: It is well known that $\pol(\Gamma)$ is a clone for all valued constraint languages $\Gamma$~\cite{Denecke-Wismath02}.
assumptions: for all valued constraint languages $\Gamma$

nodes.name: Positive weightings are necessary for tractability
nodes.statement: Positive weightings are necessary for tractability: any tractable weighted clone $W$ contains a positive weighting~\cite[Corollary 7.4]{cccjz13:sicomp}.
nodes.origin_citation: Cohen, Cooper, Creed, Jeavons & Zivny 2013, Corollary 7.4
assumptions: any tractable weighted clone $W$

nodes.name: Crisp weighted relational clones with a near-unanimity polymorphism are tractable
nodes.statement: Since crisp weighted relational clones with a near-unanimity polymorphism are tractable~\cite{Jeavons97:closure}, we get the following.
assumptions: crisp weighted relational clones with a near-unanimity polymorphism

nodes.name: Crisp weighted relational clones with a minority polymorphism are tractable
nodes.statement: Since crisp weighted relational clones with a minority polymorphism are tractable~\cite{Jeavons97:closure}, we get the following.
assumptions: crisp weighted relational clones with a minority polymorphism

nodes.name: Characterisation of tractable finite-valued constraint languages
nodes.statement: The authors have recently shown that with respect to tractability of finite-valued constraint languages the necessary and sufficient condition is having a binary weighting $\omega$ that assigns positive weight to idempotent \emph{commutative} operations only; that is, for every $f\in\supp(\omega)$ we have $f(x,y)=f(y,x)$ for all $x,y\in D$~\cite{tz13:stoc}.\footnote{The result from~\cite{tz13:stoc} extends from finite-valued constraint languages to finite-valued weighted relational clones as adding the binary equality relation and unary constant relations does not affect tractability in the presence of a binary commutative weighted polymorphism.}
nodes.statement_short: Finite-valued tractability is equivalent to having a binary weighting supported on idempotent commutative operations.
assumptions: with respect to tractability of finite-valued constraint languages
conclusions: the necessary and sufficient condition is having a binary weighting $\omega$ that assigns positive weight to idempotent \emph{commutative} operations only; that is, for every $f\in\supp(\omega)$ we have $f(x,y)=f(y,x)$ for all $x,y\in D$

nodes.name: Cyclic weighted polymorphism is necessary for tractability
nodes.statement: In recent work on the tractability of valued constraint languages, it has been shown that a necessary condition for tractability is the existence of a \emph{cyclic} weighted polymorphism~\cite{Kozik15:icalp}.
assumptions: tractability of valued constraint languages
conclusions: a necessary condition for tractability is the existence of a \emph{cyclic} weighted polymorphism

nodes.name: Cyclic weighted polymorphism is sufficient under the Feder-Vardi conjecture
nodes.statement: Moreover, it has been also shown that, under the assumption of the dichotomy conjecture of Feder and Vardi for the decision problem, this condition is also sufficient~\cite{Kolmogorov15:general-valued}.
assumptions: under the assumption of the dichotomy conjecture of Feder and Vardi for the decision problem

nodes.name: Corollary 1 (near-unanimity weighting implies tractability)
nodes.statement: A weighted clone containing a positive weighting $\omega$ with all operations in $\supp(\omega)$ being near-unanimity operations is tractable.
assumptions: A weighted clone containing a positive weighting $\omega$ with all operations in $\supp(\omega)$ being near-unanimity operations

nodes.name: Corollary 2 (minority weighting implies tractability)
nodes.statement: A weighted clone containing a positive weighting $\omega$ with all operations in $\supp(\omega)$ being minority operations is tractable.
assumptions: A weighted clone containing a positive weighting $\omega$ with all operations in $\supp(\omega)$ being minority operations

nodes.name: Corollary 3 (finite-valued weighted clones with a case (2c) weighting are tractable)
nodes.statement: A finite-valued weighted clone containing a positive weighting $\omega$ described in~Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(2c) is tractable.
assumptions: A finite-valued weighted clone containing a positive weighting $\omega$ described in~Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(2c)

nodes.name: Feasibility relations belong to weighted relational clones
nodes.statement: Note that for any weighted relational clone $\Gamma$ if $\phi\in\Gamma$ then $\feas(\phi)\in\Gamma$ as $\feas(\phi)=0\phi$.
assumptions: for any weighted relational clone $\Gamma$ if $\phi\in\Gamma$

nodes.name: Projections are trivial polymorphisms
nodes.statement: Projections are (trivial) polymorphisms of all valued constraint languages.
assumptions: all valued constraint languages

nodes.name: Superposition preserves the zero-sum condition on weightings
nodes.statement: If $\omega$ satisfies~\eqref{ineq:weightingzero} then so does $\omega[g_1,\ldots,g_k]$.
assumptions: If $\omega$ satisfies~\eqref{ineq:weightingzero}

nodes.name: Classification of ternary sharp operations into eight types
nodes.statement: Ternary sharp operations may be classified according to their labels on tuples of the form $(x,x,y), (x,y,x)$ and $(y,x,x)$, which must be equal to either $x$ or $y$. There are precisely $8$ possibilities, as listed in Table~\ref{tab:sharp3}.
assumptions: Ternary sharp operations
conclusions: may be classified according to their labels on tuples of the form $(x,x,y), (x,y,x)$ and $(y,x,x)$, which must be equal to either $x$ or $y$. There are precisely $8$ possibilities

nodes.name: Rigid cores are exactly the idempotent support clones
nodes.statement: It is not hard to show that a weighted clone $W$ (a valued constraint language $\Gamma$) is a rigid core if and only if all operations in the support clone of $W$ (polymorphisms of $\Gamma$, respectively) are idempotent.
assumptions: a weighted clone $W$ (a valued constraint language $\Gamma$)
conclusions: is a rigid core if and only if all operations in the support clone of $W$ (polymorphisms of $\Gamma$, respectively) are idempotent

nodes.name: A ternary near-unanimity operation is a majority operation
nodes.statement: Note that a ternary near-unanimity operation is a majority operation.
assumptions: a ternary near-unanimity operation

nodes.name: Finite-valued constraint languages correspond to support clone $\mathcal{O}_D$
nodes.statement: Weighted clones corresponding to finite-valued constraint languages (together with the binary equality relation $\phi_=$) are those with support clone $\mathcal{O}_D$. To see this, we denote, for a clone $C$, by $\inv(C)$ the relational clone that consists of relations $R$ with $f\in\pol(R)$ for every $f\in C$. Then, it is well known that $\inv(\mathcal{O}_D)=\relclone(\{\phi_=\})$ and observe that $\feas(\imp(W))\subseteq\inv(\mathcal{O}_D)$ for any weighted clone $W$ with support clone $\mathcal{O}_D$.
nodes.statement_short: Finite-valued languages correspond to weighted clones whose support clone is all of $\mathcal{O}_D$.
assumptions: Weighted clones corresponding to finite-valued constraint languages (together with the binary equality relation $\phi_=$)

nodes.name: $\feas(\imp(W))=\inv(C)$ for any nonempty weighted clone
nodes.statement: More generally, we have $\feas(\imp(W))=\inv(C)$ for any nonempty weighted clone $W$ with support clone $C$. On the one hand, if $\phi\in\imp(W)$ then, by Definition~\ref{def:wp}, $C\subseteq\pol(\phi)$, which implies $\feas(\phi)\in\inv(\pol(\phi))\subseteq\inv(C)$. On the other hand, if $R\in\inv(C)$ then $C\subseteq\pol(R)$. Since $R$ satisfies~\eqref{eq:WPOL} we have $R\in\imp(W)$.
nodes.statement_short: The feasibility relations of $\imp(W)$ are exactly $\inv(C)$ for the support clone $C$.
assumptions: for any nonempty weighted clone $W$ with support clone $C$

nodes.name: $\inv(\mathbf{I}_D)=\mathcal{R}$
nodes.statement: It is known that $\inv(\mathbf{I}_D)=\mathcal{R}$~\cite{Bulatov05:classifying}.

nodes.name: Weighted relational clones of finite-valued weighted clones
nodes.statement: The weighted relational clones corresponding to finite-valued weighted clones are those that are subsets of the weighted relational clone generated by $\mathcal{R}$ and finite-valued weighted relations.
assumptions: The weighted relational clones corresponding to finite-valued weighted clones
conclusions: are those that are subsets of the weighted relational clone generated by $\mathcal{R}$ and finite-valued weighted relations

nodes.name: Feasibility relations of finite-valued weighted clones lie in $\mathcal{R}$
nodes.statement: Let $W$ be a finite-valued weighted clone on $D$. Then for any weighted relation $\phi\in\imp(W)$ we have $\feas(\phi)\in\mathcal{R}$.
assumptions: Let $W$ be a finite-valued weighted clone on $D$
conclusions: for any weighted relation $\phi\in\imp(W)$ we have $\feas(\phi)\in\mathcal{R}$

nodes.name: Cases (2a) and (2b) give trivial finite-valued weighted relational clones
nodes.statement: If $W$ contains a weighting described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(2a) then, by Proposition~\ref{prop:majority}, $\imp(W)$ is crisp and thus every $\phi\in\imp(W)$ can be written as the addition of a rational constant to a weighted relation in $\mathcal{R}$. Hence $\imp(W)$ is tractable. Similarly, if $W$ contains a weighting described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(2b) then, by Proposition~\ref{prop:minority}, $\imp(W)$ is crisp and thus every $\phi\in\imp(W)$ can be written as the addition of a rational constant to a weighted relation in $\mathcal{R}$. Hence $\imp(W)$ is tractable.
nodes.statement_short: In the finite-valued case, cases (2a) and (2b) make every improved relation a constant shift of a relation in $\mathcal{R}$, hence tractable.
assumptions: If $W$ contains a weighting described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(2a)
if $W$ contains a weighting described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(2b)
conclusions: $\imp(W)$ is crisp and thus every $\phi\in\imp(W)$ can be written as the addition of a rational constant to a weighted relation in $\mathcal{R}$. Hence $\imp(W)$ is tractable

nodes.name: Weighted relational clones generating $\wrel_D$ are NP-hard
nodes.statement: Any weighted relational clone $\Gamma\subseteq\wrel_D$ with $\wrelclone(\Gamma)=\wrel_D$ is NP-hard.
assumptions: Any weighted relational clone $\Gamma\subseteq\wrel_D$ with $\wrelclone(\Gamma)=\wrel_D$

nodes.name: Maximality of a language equals maximality of its weighted relational clone
nodes.statement: It follows that a valued constraint language $\Gamma$ is maximal if and only if the weighted relational clone $\wrelclone(\Gamma)$ is maximal.
assumptions: a valued constraint language $\Gamma$
conclusions: is maximal if and only if the weighted relational clone $\wrelclone(\Gamma)$ is maximal

nodes.name: Maximal relational clones as a special case
nodes.statement: As a special case of Definition~\ref{def:maximal}, we get that a relational clone $\Gamma$ is maximal if $\Gamma\neq\rel_D$ but for any $R\in\rel_D$ we have $\relclone(\Gamma\cup\{R\})=\rel_D$.
assumptions: a relational clone $\Gamma$
conclusions: is maximal if $\Gamma\neq\rel_D$ but for any $R\in\rel_D$ we have $\relclone(\Gamma\cup\{R\})=\rel_D$

nodes.name: Maximal weighted relational clones correspond to minimal weighted clones
nodes.statement: Maximal weighted relational clones correspond, via the Galois correspondence given in Theorem~\ref{thm:wgc}, to minimal weighted clones.
assumptions: Maximal weighted relational clones
conclusions: correspond, via the Galois correspondence given in Theorem~\ref{thm:wgc}, to minimal weighted clones

nodes.name: Cyclic permutation moves between Pixley types
nodes.statement: For any Pixley operation $f$ of type $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ we can obtain, by (cyclically) permuting the arguments of $f$, Pixley operations of the other two types. For instance, if $f\in\mbox{P1}$ then we have $g\in\mbox{P2}$ and $h\in\mbox{P3}$, where $g(x,y,z)=f[\proj^{(3)}_3,\proj^{(3)}_1,\proj^{(3)}_2]=f(z,x,y)$ and $h(x,y,z)=f[\proj^{(3)}_2,\proj^{(3)}_3,\proj^{(3)}_1]=f(y,z,x)$.
assumptions: For any Pixley operation $f$ of type $i\in\{1,2,3\}$
conclusions: we can obtain, by (cyclically) permuting the arguments of $f$, Pixley operations of the other two types

nodes.name: Superposition table for ternary sharp operations
nodes.statement: The following table, which can be verified using the definitions above, will be useful in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}. It lists the types of ternary sharp operations obtained by superposing a ternary sharp operation of an arbitrary type (columns in Table~\ref{tab:types}) with any of the three cyclic permutations of the three ternary projections (rows in Table~\ref{tab:types}).
assumptions: a ternary sharp operation of an arbitrary type
any of the three cyclic permutations of the three ternary projections
conclusions: the types of ternary sharp operations obtained by superposing

nodes.name: Case (2c) weightings imply tractability
nodes.statement: In a recent paper the authors have shown~\cite{tz15:icalp} that any weighting described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(2c) implies tractability. This is a corollary of the following result.
assumptions: any weighting described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(2c)

nodes.name: Dichotomy conjecture of Feder and Vardi
nodes.statement: the conjecture of Feder and Vardi~\cite{Feder98:monotone}, which asserts that every constraint language is either tractable or NP-hard, and its algebraic refinement, which specifies the precise boundary between tractable and NP-hard languages~\cite{Bulatov05:classifying}
nodes.statement_short: Every constraint language is either tractable or NP-hard.
nodes.origin_citation: Feder & Vardi 1998; algebraic refinement Bulatov, Krokhin & Jeavons 2005
assumptions: every constraint language

nodes.name: Fixed finite domain $D$
nodes.statement: Throughout the paper, let $D$ be a fixed finite set of size at least two.

nodes.name: Only weighted clones with a positive weighting are considered
nodes.statement: Consequently, throughout this paper we will be only concerned with weighted clones that contain a positive weighting.

nodes.name: valued constraint satisfaction problem (VCSP)
nodes.statement: An instance of the \emph{valued constraint satisfaction problem} (VCSP) is specified by a finite set $V=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$ of variables, a finite set $D$ of labels, and an \emph{objective function} $\inst$ expressed as follows: \begin{equation} \inst(x_1,\ldots, x_n)=\sum_{i=1}^q{\phi_i(\tup{x}_i)}\,, \end{equation} where each $\phi_i(\tup{x}_i)$, $1\le i\le q$, is a valued constraint over $V$. Each constraint can appear multiple times in $\inst$. The goal is to find an \emph{assignment} (or a \emph{labelling}) of labels to the variables that minimises $\inst$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimise a sum of weighted relations applied to scopes of variables over a finite label set.

nodes.name: Coordinatewise application of a $k$-ary operation to $m$-tuples
nodes.statement: We will apply a $k$-ary operation $f$ to $k$ $m$-tuples $\tup{x_1},\ldots,\tup{x_k}\in D^m$ coordinatewise, that is, \begin{equation} f(\tup{x_1},\ldots,\tup{x_k})=(f(\tup{x_1}[1],\ldots,\tup{x_k}[1]),\ldots,f(\tup{x_1}[m],\ldots,\tup{x_k}[m]))\,. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Entry notation $\tup{x}[i]$ for tuples
nodes.statement: Given an $m$-tuple $\tup{x}\in D^m$, we denote its $i$th entry by $\tup{x}[i]$ for $1\leq i\leq m$.

nodes.name: Extended rationals $\qq$
nodes.statement: Let $\qq=\mathbb{Q}\cup\{\infty\}$ denote the set of rational numbers with (positive) infinity.

nodes.name: Binary equality relation $\phi_=$
nodes.statement: An important example of a (weighted) relation is the binary equality $\phi_=$ on $D$: $\phi_=(x,y)=0$ if $x=y$ and $\phi_=(x,y)=\infty$ if $x\neq y$.

nodes.name: Max-Cut as a VCSP instance
nodes.statement: The \textsc{Max-Cut} problem for a graph is to find a cut with the largest possible size. This problem is NP-hard~\cite{Garey79:intractability} and equivalent to the \textsc{Min-UnCut} problem with respect to exact solvability. For a graph $(V,E)$ with $V=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$, this problem can be expressed as the VCSP instance $\inst(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{(i,j)\in E} \phi_{\sf xor}(x_i,x_j)$ over the Boolean domain $D=\{0,1\}$, where $\phi_{\sf xor}:\{0,1\}^2\to\qq$ is defined by $\phi_{\sf xor}(x,y)=1$ if $x=y$ and $\phi_{\sf xor}(x,y)=0$ if $x\neq y$.
nodes.statement_short: Max-Cut is the VCSP over $\{\phi_{\sf xor}\}$ on the Boolean domain.

nodes.name: The clones $\mathbf{J}_D$ and $\mathcal{O}_D$
nodes.statement: For any $D$, let $\mathbf{J}_D$ be the set of all projections on $D$ and $\mathcal{O}_D$ be the set of all operations on $D$. By Definition~\ref{def:clone}, both $\mathbf{J}_D$ and $\mathcal{O}_D$ are clones.

nodes.name: The weighted clones $\mathbf{W}_C^0$ and $\mathbf{W}_C$
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a clone. We give examples of two weighted clones with support clone $C$. \begin{enumerate} \item $\mathbf{W}_C^0$ is the zero-valued weighted clone, that is, the weighted clone containing, for each arity $k$, a weighting $\omega_k\in\mathbf{W}_C^0$ with $\omega_k(f)=0$ for all $f\in C^{(k)}$. \item $\mathbf{W}_C$ is the weighted clone containing all possible weightings of $C$. \end{enumerate} By Definition~\ref{ex:wclones}, weighted clones are closed under nonnegative scaling. Consequently, by scaling by zero, any weighted clone $W$ with support clone $C$ contains $\mathbf{W}_C^0$, which is the inclusion-wise smallest weighted clone with support clone $C$. On the other hand, $\mathbf{W}_C$ is the inclusion-wise largest weighted clone with support clone $C$.
nodes.statement_short: The zero-valued weighted clone is smallest and the all-weightings clone $\mathbf{W}_C$ is largest with support clone $C$.

nodes.name: $\supp(W)\cup\mathbf{J}_D$ is a clone
nodes.statement: It is easy to show that $\supp(W)\cup\mathbf{J}_D$ is a clone for any weighted clone $W$ defined on $D$~\cite{cccjz13:sicomp}, see also~\cite{Kozik15:icalp,tz15:icalp}.

nodes.name: Submodular functions and the weighted polymorphism $\omega_{sub}$
nodes.statement: Consider the class of submodular functions~\cite{Nemhauser88:optimization}. These are precisely the functions $\phi$ defined on $D=\{0,1\}$ satisfying $\phi(\min(\tup{x}_1,\tup{x}_2)) + \phi(\max(\tup{x}_1,\tup{x}_2)) - \phi(\tup{x}_1) - \phi(\tup{x}_2) \leq 0$, where $\min$ and $\max$ are the two binary operations that return the smaller and larger of its two arguments respectively with respect to the usual order $0<1$. In other words, the set of submodular functions is the set of weighted relations with a binary weighted polymorphism $\omega_{sub}$ defined by: $\omega_{sub}(f)=-1$ if $f \in \{e_1^{(2)},e_2^{(2)}\}$, $\omega_{sub}(f)=+1$ if $f \in \{\min,\max\}$, and $\omega_{sub}(f)=0$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Submodularity is exactly having the binary weighted polymorphism $\omega_{sub}$ supported on $\{\min,\max\}$.

nodes.name: $\imp$ of the extreme weighted clones
nodes.statement: Every weighting in $\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{J}_D}^0$ is a weighted polymorphism of any possible weighted relation. Hence $\imp(\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{J}_D}^0)=\wrel_D$. The weighted relations that are improved by all weightings are precisely those which take at most one value. Hence $\imp(\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{J}_D})=\rel_D$.

nodes.name: Tournament operation gives a tractable weighted clone
nodes.statement: A binary operation $f:D^2\rightarrow D$ is called conservative if $f(x,y)\in\{x,y\}$ for all $x,y\in D$ and commutative if $f(x,y)=f(y,x)$ for all $x,y\in D$. Moreover, $f$ is called a \emph{tournament} operation if $f$ is both conservative and commutative. Let $W$ be a weighted clone such $\supp(W)$ contains a tournament operation. Then, by a recent result of the authors~\cite{tz15:icalp}, $W$ is tractable.
nodes.statement_short: A tournament operation in the support makes the weighted clone tractable.

nodes.name: Rectangular band giving an intractable weighted clone
nodes.statement: Let $D=\{0,1,2,3\}$ and let $f$ be a binary operation defined by Table~\ref{table:bin}. \begin{table}[hbt] \begin{center} \begin{tabular}{c|cccc} \textbf{f} & \textbf{0} & \textbf{1} & \textbf{2} & \textbf{3} \\ \hline \textbf{0} & 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ \textbf{1} & 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ \textbf{2} & 2 & 3 & 2 & 3 \\ \textbf{3} & 2 & 3 & 2 & 3 \end{tabular} \end{center} \caption{Definition of $f$ from Example~\ref{ex:f}.} \end{table} Note that $f$ is an idempotent operation but not a projection. In fact, $f$ is an example of a \emph{rectangular band}~\cite{McKenzie87:algebras}, which is an idempotent and associative binary operation $f:D^2\to D$ satisfying $f(x,f(y,z))=f(x,z)$ for all $x,y,z\in D$. Let $W$ be the weighted clone generated by the weighting $\omega$ defined by $\omega(\proj^{(2)}_1)=\omega(\proj^{(2)}_2)=-1$ and $\omega(f)=+2$. It is known that $W$ is intractable~\cite{Jeavons97:closure,Pearson97:survey}.
nodes.statement_short: A rectangular band on a 4-element domain generates an intractable weighted clone with a case (1) weighting.

nodes.name: Multimorphisms of case (2c) type imply tractability
nodes.statement: A $k$-ary weighting $\omega$ is a \emph{multimorphism} if $\omega(f)\in\mathbb{N}$ for all $f\in\supp(\omega)$ and $\omega(\proj^{(k)}_i)=-1$ for all $1\leq i\leq k$~\cite{Cohen06:complexitysoft}. It has been shown that if a weighted clone $W$ contains a weighting $\omega$ described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(2c) such that $\omega$ is a multimorphism then $W$ is tractable~\cite{kz13:jacm}.
nodes.origin_citation: Cohen, Cooper, Jeavons & Krokhin 2006; Kolmogorov & Zivny 2013

nodes.name: Not-All-Equal Satisfiability: semiprojections alone do not imply tractability
nodes.statement: Let $D$ be a fixed set with $|D|>2$. Fix two distinct labels from $D$, say $0,1\in D$. Let $\phi$ be the following ternary weighted relation: $\phi(x,y,z)=\infty$ if $\{x,y,z\}=\{0\}$, or $\{x,y,z\}=\{1\}$, or $\{x,y,z\}\neq\{0,1\}$; and $\phi(x,y,z)=0$ otherwise. The weighted relation $\phi$ corresponds to the \textsc{Not-All-Equal Satisfiability} problem~\cite{Garey79:intractability}, which is NP-hard~\cite{Schaefer78:complexity}. It is easy to show that every semiprojection on $D$ is a polymorphism of $\phi$. Take a $k$-ary semiprojection $f$ for some $k\geq 3$ and $\tup{x}_1,\ldots,\tup{x}_k\in\feas(\phi)$. From the definition of $\phi$, we have $\tup{x}_i\in\{0,1\}^3$ for every $1\leq i\leq k$. Since there are at most two distinct labels in each coordinate, $f(\tup{x}_1,\ldots,\tup{x}_k)$ reduces to a projection (from the definition of semiprojections) and thus $f$ is a polymorphism of $\phi$ as $f(\tup{x}_1,\ldots,\tup{x}_k)=\tup{x}_i$ for some $1\leq i\leq k$. Let $C$ be the clone of operations on $D$ generated by all semiprojections on $D$. Let $W=\mathbf{W}_C$ be the weighted clone containing all possible weightings of $C$. In particular, $W$ contains all possible weightings whose support contains only semiprojections. Since $C\subseteq\pol(\phi)$ and $\phi$ is a relation we have that $\phi\in\imp(W)$. Consequently, $W$ is intractable.
nodes.statement_short: The NP-hard Not-All-Equal-Sat relation is improved by the weighted clone generated by all semiprojections, so case (3) alone is insufficient.

nodes.name: An intractable finite-valued weighted clone with a case (1) weighting
nodes.statement: Let $D=\{0,1,2\}$. Recall from Example~\ref{ex:TP} that a binary operation $f:D^2\to D$ is \emph{conservative} if $f(x,y)\in\{x,y\}$ for all $x,y\in D$. For any conservative binary operation $f:D^2\to D$ and any 2-element subdomain $\{a,b\}\subseteq D$, the restriction $\Crestrict{f}{\{a,b\}}$ of $f$ onto $\{a,b\}$ behaves either as $\proj^{(2)}_1$, $\proj^{(2)}_2$, $\min$, or $\max$, where $\min$ and $\max$ are the two operations that return the smaller (larger) of its two arguments with respect to the usual order $0<1<2$, respectively. Consider the operations in Table~\ref{table:w} described by their behaviour on the various 2-element subdomains. \begin{table}[htb] \begin{center} \begin{tabular}{lccc|l} $\mathbf{f}$ & \{\textbf{0},\textbf{1}\} & \{\textbf{0},\textbf{2}\} & \{\textbf{1},\textbf{2}\} & $\mathbf{\omega(f)}$\\ \hline $f_1$ & $\proj^{(2)}_1$ & $\proj^{(2)}_1$ & $\proj^{(2)}_1$ & -0.5 \\ $f_2$ & $\proj^{(2)}_2$ & $\proj^{(2)}_2$ & $\proj^{(2)}_2$ & -0.5 \\ $f_3$ & $\proj^{(2)}_1$ & $\min$ & $\proj^{(2)}_1$ & 0.5 \\ $f_4$ & $\proj^{(2)}_2$ & $\min$ & $\proj^{(2)}_2$ & 0.5 \\ \end{tabular} \end{center} \caption{Definition of $\omega$} \end{table} Note that $f_1=\proj^{(2)}_1$ and $f_{2}=\proj^{(2)}_2$. The weighting $\omega$ is defined by the last column of Table~\ref{table:w}. Note that $\omega$ is not commutative. It can be checked that $\omega$ is a weighted polymorphism of the finite-valued weighted relation $\phi : \{0,1,2\} \to \Q$ defined in Table~\ref{table:phi}. \begin{table}[hbt] \begin{center} \begin{tabular}{c|ccc} $\phi$ & \textbf{0} & \textbf{1} & \textbf{2} \\ \hline \textbf{0} & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ \textbf{1} & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ \textbf{2} & 1 & 1 & 1 \end{tabular} \end{center} \caption{Definition of $\phi$} \end{table} Now since $\argmin \phi=\{(0,1),(1,0)\}$, we have that $\phi$ satisfies the (MC) condition~\cite{tz13:stoc} and thus can be used to reduce from Max-Cut~\cite{Cohen06:complexitysoft}. Thus, $W=\wclone(\{\omega\})$ is intractable.
nodes.statement_short: A non-commutative binary weighting on a 3-element domain improves a finite-valued relation reducible from Max-Cut, hence generates an intractable finite-valued weighted clone.

nodes.name: Boundary of tractability for case (1) weightings
nodes.statement: A weighting described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(1) can lead both to tractable and intractable weighted clones, as the next two examples demonstrate, but the precise boundary of tractability is currently unknown.

nodes.name: Boundary of tractability for case (3) weightings
nodes.statement: We show that the weightings described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(3) \emph{alone} are not sufficient for tractability. As in case~(1), the precise boundary of tractability is currently unknown.

nodes.name: Interplay of case (1) and case (3) of Theorem 5
nodes.statement: However, the precise interplay of case~(1) and case~(3) of Theorem~\ref{thm:class2} is currently unknown.

nodes.name: Structure of weighted clones of finite-valued constraint languages
nodes.statement: However, understanding the structure of weighted clones appears a difficult problem in general. For instance, whilst the computational complexity of finite-valued constraint languages is well understood~\cite{tz13:stoc}, the structure of the corresponding weighted clones is not, as discussed in Section~\ref{sec:wclones}.

nodes.name: Equivalence with the subset definition of a relation
nodes.statement: An $m$-ary relation over $D$ is commonly defined as a subset of $D^m$. Note that Definition~\ref{def:rel} is equivalent to the standard definition as any subset of $D^m$ can be associated with the set $\{\tup{x}\in D^m\:|\:\phi(\tup{x})<\infty\}$. Consequently, we shall use both definitions interchangeably.

nodes.name: Relations as a special type of weighted relation
nodes.statement: From Definition~\ref{def:wrel} we have that relations are a special type of weighted relations. If needed we call a weighted relation \emph{unweighted} to emphasise the fact that $\phi$ is a relation.

nodes.name: Domain, labels and values terminology
nodes.statement: We call $D$ the \emph{domain}, the elements of $D$ \emph{labels} (for variables), and say that the weighted relation in $\wrel_D$ take \emph{values}.

nodes.name: CSPs as a special case of VCSPs
nodes.statement: CSPs are a special case of VCSPs with (unweighted) relations with the goal to determine the existence of a feasible solution.

nodes.name: $\{\phi_{\sf xor}\}$ is an intractable finite-valued language
nodes.statement: Example~\ref{ex:maxcut} shows that the finite-valued constraint language $\{\phi_{\sf xor}\}$ is intractable.

nodes.name: Superposition of a weighting as matrix multiplication
nodes.statement: We remark that the superposition (of an operation with other operations) is also known as composition. On the other hand, the superposition of a $k$-ary weighting $\omega$ with $k$ $\ell$-ary operations $g_1,\ldots,g_k$ can be seen as multiplying $\omega$, seen as a (row) vector, by a matrix with rows indexed by $k$-ary operations and columns indexed by $\ell$-ary operations; given a row operation $f$ and a column operation $f'$ the corresponding entry in the matrix is 1 if $f[g_1,\ldots,g_k]=f'$ and 0 otherwise. The result of this matrix multiplication is a vector of weights assigned to $\ell$-ary operations.
nodes.statement_short: Superposition of a weighting is a vector-matrix product over the incidence matrix of superposition.

nodes.name: It suffices to consider languages of the form $\imp(W)$
nodes.statement: Thus, when trying to identify tractable valued constraint languages, it is sufficient to consider only languages of the form $\imp(W)$ for some weighted clone $W$.

nodes.name: Origin of the notion of cores
nodes.statement: The idea of cores and rigid cores originated in the algebraic approach to CSPs~\cite{Jeavons98:algebraic,Bulatov05:classifying} and has also proved useful in the complexity classification of finite-valued CSPs~\cite{hkp14:sicomp,tz13:stoc}.

nodes.name: Theorem 2 was obtained independently
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:squash} was independently obtained in~\cite{Kozik15:icalp}, where it was also shown that, with respect to tractability, it suffices to restrict to rigid cores.

nodes.name: Case (3) of Theorem 5 has a non-strict arity bound
nodes.statement: Note that compared to Theorem~\ref{thm:class1} the inequality in case~(3) of Theorem~\ref{thm:class2} is not strict as it includes one of the ternary cases.

nodes.name: Theorem 5 holds for any support clone
nodes.statement: We remark that Theorem~\ref{thm:class2} holds for \emph{any} weighted clone $W$ with \emph{any} support clone $C$ as long as $W$ contains a positive weighting.

nodes.name: Consequences of Theorem 5
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:class2} tells us that (i) Pixley operations are not necessary for tractability, (ii) semiprojections can be separated from the other types of ternary operations, and (iii) the only possible interplay between majority and minority operations, as described in case~(2c) of Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}.

nodes.name: Only the multimorphism special case of (2c) was previously known
nodes.statement: Previously, only a special type of the weightings described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(2c) has been known to imply tractability.

nodes.name: Clones and purely decision problems
nodes.statement: Recall that valued constraint languages capture both decision and optimisation problems. Clones, which capture crisp valued constraint languages and thus purely decision problems, have been studied extensively in universal algebra~\cite{Szendrei86:clones,Hobby88:structure}. We now focus on an important special type of weighted clones that correspond to valued constraint languages that capture purely optimisation problems. Such valued constraint languages are called \emph{finite-valued} as they only contain finite-valued weighted relations.
nodes.statement_short: Motivation for finite-valued weighted clones as the purely optimisation counterpart of clones.

nodes.name: Rigid cores allow defining finite-valued via $\mathbf{I}_D$
nodes.statement: However, as we have limited our scope to rigid cores (which, by Theorem~\ref{thm:rigid}, does not change tractability), we will define a weighted clone $W$ to be finite-valued if its support clone is equal to $\mathbf{I}_D$, the clone of all \emph{idempotent} operations on $D$.

nodes.name: Example 9's intractability argument is not finite-valued
nodes.statement: We now give an example of an \emph{intractable finite-valued} weighted clone with a weighting as described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(1). (We note that the intractability of the weighted clone $W$ from Example~\ref{ex:f}, which contains a weighting as described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(1), relies on the fact that $W$ is not finite-valued and thus is not immediately applicable here.)

nodes.name: Case (1) weightings give both tractable and intractable finite-valued weighted clones
nodes.statement: Thus weightings described in Theorem~\ref{thm:class2}\,(1) can lead to both tractable and intractable finite-valued weighted clones.

nodes.name: Maximal crisp weighted relational clones are already classified
nodes.statement: Maximal crisp weighted relational clones have been classified with respect to tractability in~\cite{Bulatov01:complexity,Bulatov04:graph}.

nodes.name: Types are not preserved jointly under permutation
nodes.statement: Note that taking a semiprojection $f$ of type $i$ and a Pixley operation $g$ of type $i$, $f^\pi$ and $g^\pi$ can be of different types; e.g., if $f$ is a semiprojection of type $1$ and $g$ is a Pixley operation of type $1$ and $\pi=(2,3,1)$ then $f^\pi$ is a semiprojection of type $2$ and $g^\pi$ is a Pixley operation of type $3$.

nodes.name: Concluding summary of the technique
nodes.statement: We have presented new results on the structure of weighted clones that delimit the possibilities for tractable valued constraint languages. In order to establish our results, we have presented a novel technique for ruling out certain types of operations from the support of a given weighting. The method considers certain extreme cases of the dual of the linear program that demonstrates the existence of a weighted sum of superpositions that assigns zero weight to the forbidden operations. We believe that our results and techniques will prove useful in further studies of the structure of weighted clones.
nodes.statement_short: The novel technique uses LP duality to build a weighted sum of superpositions that zeroes out forbidden operations.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Let \begin{equation} \omega'\ =\ \sum_{\pi\in\perm_k}\omega[\proj^{(k)}_{\pi(1)},\ldots,\proj^{(k)}_{\pi(k)}]\,. \end{equation} Let $f\in\supp(\omega)$ and $\pi\in\perm_k$. We have \begin{multline} \omega'(f)\ =\ \sum_{g\in\supp(\omega)}\ \sum_{\substack{\text{$\sigma\in\perm_k$}\\\text{$g^{\sigma}=f$}}}\omega(g) \ =\ \sum_{g\in\supp(\omega)}\ \sum_{\substack{\text{$\sigma\circ\pi\in\perm_k$}\\\text{$g^{\sigma\circ\pi}=f^\pi$}}}\omega(g) \ =\ \\ \ =\ \sum_{g\in\supp(\omega)}\ \sum_{\substack{\text{$\sigma'\in\perm_k$}\\\text{$g^{\sigma'}=f^\pi$}}}\omega(g) \ = \ \omega'(f^\pi)\,. \end{multline} Thus $\omega'$ satisfies the first and the third property of the lemma. Since $\omega$ is positive we have that $\sum_{i=1}^k\omega(\proj^{(k)}_i)<0$ and thus, by~\eqref{eq:long}, we have $\omega'(\proj^{(k)}_i)<0$ for every $1\leq i\leq k$. Let $\omega'(\proj^{(k)}_1)=w$. By~\eqref{eq:long} again, $\omega'(\proj^{(k)}_i)=w$ for every $1\leq i\leq k$. Thus $\mu=\frac{1}{w}\omega'$ satisfies all three properties of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Average $\omega$ over all cyclic permutations of its arguments, then rescale so that each projection gets weight $-1$.

nodes.name: Define the cyclically symmetrised weighting
nodes.statement: Let \begin{equation} \omega'\ =\ \sum_{\pi\in\perm_k}\omega[\proj^{(k)}_{\pi(1)},\ldots,\proj^{(k)}_{\pi(k)}]\,. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $\omega'$ as the sum of superpositions of $\omega$ with all cyclic permutations of the projections.

nodes.name: Verify permutation invariance of $\omega'$
nodes.statement: Let $f\in\supp(\omega)$ and $\pi\in\perm_k$. We have \begin{multline} \omega'(f)\ =\ \sum_{g\in\supp(\omega)}\ \sum_{\substack{\text{$\sigma\in\perm_k$}\\\text{$g^{\sigma}=f$}}}\omega(g) \ =\ \sum_{g\in\supp(\omega)}\ \sum_{\substack{\text{$\sigma\circ\pi\in\perm_k$}\\\text{$g^{\sigma\circ\pi}=f^\pi$}}}\omega(g) \ =\ \\ \ =\ \sum_{g\in\supp(\omega)}\ \sum_{\substack{\text{$\sigma'\in\perm_k$}\\\text{$g^{\sigma'}=f^\pi$}}}\omega(g) \ = \ \omega'(f^\pi)\,. \end{multline} Thus $\omega'$ satisfies the first and the third property of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Reindex the double sum by $\sigma\circ\pi$ to obtain $\omega'(f)=\omega'(f^\pi)$, giving properties 1 and 3.

nodes.name: Normalise the projection weights
nodes.statement: Since $\omega$ is positive we have that $\sum_{i=1}^k\omega(\proj^{(k)}_i)<0$ and thus, by~\eqref{eq:long}, we have $\omega'(\proj^{(k)}_i)<0$ for every $1\leq i\leq k$. Let $\omega'(\proj^{(k)}_1)=w$. By~\eqref{eq:long} again, $\omega'(\proj^{(k)}_i)=w$ for every $1\leq i\leq k$. Thus $\mu=\frac{1}{w}\omega'$ satisfies all three properties of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Scale $\omega'$ by $1/w$, where $w$ is the common (negative) projection weight, to get $\mu$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Let $\omega\in\wpol(\Gamma)$ be a positive unary weighting. By scaling by $1/|\omega(\proj^{(1)}_1)|$, we have $\omega(\proj^{(1)}_1)=-1$ and thus $\sum_{f\in\supp(\omega)}\omega(f)=1$. For any weighted relation $\phi\in\Gamma$ of arity $m$ and any $m$-tuple $\tup{x}\in D^m$, we have $(\ast)$ $\phi(\tup{x})\geq\sum_{f\in\supp(\omega)}\omega(f)\phi(f(\tup{x}))$. Suppose that $\tup{y}$ is a minimal-cost assignment for $\phi$; that is, $\phi(\tup{y})\leq\phi(\tup{x})$ for all $\tup{x}\in D^m$. Then for every $f\in\supp(\omega)$, we have $f(\tup{y})$ is also a minimal-cost assignment. Assume for contrary that for some $f'\in\supp(\omega)$, we have $\phi(f'(\tup{y}))>\phi(\tup{y})$; write $\phi(f'(\tup{y}))=\phi(\tup{y})+\epsilon$, where $\epsilon>0$. Then we claim that there is an $f\in\supp(\omega)$ such that $\phi(f(\tup{y}))<\phi(\tup{y})$, which contradicts the choice of $\tup{y}$. To prove the claim assume that $\phi(f(\tup{y}))\geq\phi(\tup{y})$ for every $f\in\supp(\omega)\setminus\{f'\}$. Hence we get $\sum_{f\in\supp(\omega)}\omega(f)\phi(f(\tup{y})) = \sum_{f\in\supp(\omega)\setminus\{f'\}}\omega(f)\phi(f(\tup{y}))+\omega(f')\phi(f'(\tup{y})) \geq (1-\omega(f')\phi(\tup{y})+\omega(f')(\phi(\tup{y})+\epsilon) = \phi(\tup{y})+\omega(f')\epsilon>\phi(\tup{y})$, which contradicts $(\ast)$. Consequently, given an instance $I\in\VCSP(\Gamma)$ and a solution $s$ to $I$, we can take any unary weighting $\omega\in\wpol(\Gamma)$ and any unary operation $f\in\supp(\omega)$ and get another solution $f(s)$ to $I$; the solution $f(s)$ uses only labels from $f(D)$. Consider a unary non-bijective operation $f\in\supp(\omega)$ with the minimum $|f(D)|$ over all unary weightings $\omega\in\wpol(\Gamma)$. We denote by $D'=f(D)$ the range of $f$. We denote by $\Gamma'$ language containing the restriction of every $\phi\in\Gamma$ to $D'$. Given any instance $I\in\VCSP(\Gamma)$ we can create, by replacing each weighted relation $\phi$ in $I$ by $\phi'$, in polynomial time an instance $I'\in\VCSP(\Gamma')$ with the following properties: any solution to $I'$ is also a solution to $I$, and for any solution $s$ to $I$ we have that $f(s)$ is a solution to $I'$. If $\Gamma'$ is not a core we can repeat the same construction with $\Gamma'$.
nodes.statement_short: A positive unary weighting maps optimal assignments to optimal assignments, so restricting the language to the range of a minimal non-bijective $f\in\supp(\omega)$ preserves complexity.

nodes.name: Normalise the unary weighting and record the averaging inequality
nodes.statement: Let $\omega\in\wpol(\Gamma)$ be a positive unary weighting. By scaling by $1/|\omega(\proj^{(1)}_1)|$, we have $\omega(\proj^{(1)}_1)=-1$ and thus $\sum_{f\in\supp(\omega)}\omega(f)=1$. For any weighted relation $\phi\in\Gamma$ of arity $m$ and any $m$-tuple $\tup{x}\in D^m$, we have $(\ast)$ $\phi(\tup{x})\geq\sum_{f\in\supp(\omega)}\omega(f)\phi(f(\tup{x}))$.
nodes.statement_short: Scale so $\omega(\proj^{(1)}_1)=-1$, giving the inequality $(\ast)$ bounding $\phi(\tup{x})$ from below.

nodes.name: Optimal assignments are preserved by the support operations
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\tup{y}$ is a minimal-cost assignment for $\phi$; that is, $\phi(\tup{y})\leq\phi(\tup{x})$ for all $\tup{x}\in D^m$. Then for every $f\in\supp(\omega)$, we have $f(\tup{y})$ is also a minimal-cost assignment. Assume for contrary that for some $f'\in\supp(\omega)$, we have $\phi(f'(\tup{y}))>\phi(\tup{y})$; write $\phi(f'(\tup{y}))=\phi(\tup{y})+\epsilon$, where $\epsilon>0$. Then we claim that there is an $f\in\supp(\omega)$ such that $\phi(f(\tup{y}))<\phi(\tup{y})$, which contradicts the choice of $\tup{y}$. To prove the claim assume that $\phi(f(\tup{y}))\geq\phi(\tup{y})$ for every $f\in\supp(\omega)\setminus\{f'\}$. Hence we get $\sum_{f\in\supp(\omega)}\omega(f)\phi(f(\tup{y})) = \sum_{f\in\supp(\omega)\setminus\{f'\}}\omega(f)\phi(f(\tup{y}))+\omega(f')\phi(f'(\tup{y})) \geq (1-\omega(f')\phi(\tup{y})+\omega(f')(\phi(\tup{y})+\epsilon) = \phi(\tup{y})+\omega(f')\epsilon>\phi(\tup{y})$, which contradicts $(\ast)$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume some $f'$ strictly increases the cost of a minimiser and derive a contradiction with $(\ast)$.

nodes.name: Solutions can be pushed into the range of $f$
nodes.statement: Consequently, given an instance $I\in\VCSP(\Gamma)$ and a solution $s$ to $I$, we can take any unary weighting $\omega\in\wpol(\Gamma)$ and any unary operation $f\in\supp(\omega)$ and get another solution $f(s)$ to $I$; the solution $f(s)$ uses only labels from $f(D)$.
nodes.statement_short: Any solution $s$ of an instance yields the solution $f(s)$ using only labels from $f(D)$.

nodes.name: Construct the smaller domain $D'$ and language $\Gamma'$
nodes.statement: Consider a unary non-bijective operation $f\in\supp(\omega)$ with the minimum $|f(D)|$ over all unary weightings $\omega\in\wpol(\Gamma)$. We denote by $D'=f(D)$ the range of $f$. We denote by $\Gamma'$ language containing the restriction of every $\phi\in\Gamma$ to $D'$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick a non-bijective $f\in\supp(\omega)$ minimising $|f(D)|$ and restrict every $\phi\in\Gamma$ to $D'=f(D)$.

nodes.name: Polynomial-time reduction between the two languages and iteration
nodes.statement: Given any instance $I\in\VCSP(\Gamma)$ we can create, by replacing each weighted relation $\phi$ in $I$ by $\phi'$, in polynomial time an instance $I'\in\VCSP(\Gamma')$ with the following properties: any solution to $I'$ is also a solution to $I$, and for any solution $s$ to $I$ we have that $f(s)$ is a solution to $I'$. If $\Gamma'$ is not a core we can repeat the same construction with $\Gamma'$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewriting instances gives mutual solution transfer; iterate if $\Gamma'$ is still not a core.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 7
nodes.statement: Let $\omega$ be $k$-ary. Note that if $f$ is a $k$-ary near-unanimity operation then so is $g(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=f(x_{\pi(1)},\ldots,x_{\pi(k)})$ for any permutation $\pi$ on $\{1,\ldots,k\}$. Thus, by Lemma~\ref{lem:perm}, we can assume $\omega$ assigns weight $-1$ to each of the $k$ projections (and still every $f\in\supp(\omega)$ is a near-unanimity operation). Let $\phi\in\imp(W)$ be an $m$-ary weighted relation and let $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in D^m$ be such that $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in\dom(\phi)$. Since $\omega\in\wpol(\phi)$, we have, by~\eqref{eq:WPOL} with $\tup{x}_1=\tup{y}$ and $\tup{x}_i=\tup{x}$ for all $2\leq i\leq k$, and by~\eqref{eq:defNU}, $-\phi(\tup{y})-(k-1)\phi(\tup{x})+k\phi(\tup{x})\leq 0$, which gives $\phi(\tup{x})\leq\phi(\tup{y})$. By swapping $\tup{x}$ and $\tup{y}$ in~\eqref{eq:WPOL}, we get $-\phi(\tup{x})-(k-1)\phi(\tup{y})+k\phi(\tup{y})\leq 0$, which gives $\phi(\tup{y})\leq\phi(\tup{x})$. Together, $\phi(\tup{x})=\phi(\tup{y})$ for all $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in\dom(\phi)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the weighted-polymorphism inequality to the tuple pattern $(\tup{y},\tup{x},\ldots,\tup{x})$ and its swap to force $\phi(\tup{x})=\phi(\tup{y})$.

nodes.name: Normalise $\omega$ using Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Let $\omega$ be $k$-ary. Note that if $f$ is a $k$-ary near-unanimity operation then so is $g(x_1,\ldots,x_k)=f(x_{\pi(1)},\ldots,x_{\pi(k)})$ for any permutation $\pi$ on $\{1,\ldots,k\}$. Thus, by Lemma~\ref{lem:perm}, we can assume $\omega$ assigns weight $-1$ to each of the $k$ projections (and still every $f\in\supp(\omega)$ is a near-unanimity operation).
nodes.statement_short: Near-unanimity is permutation-closed, so Lemma 2 lets us assume weight $-1$ on every projection.

nodes.name: Instantiate the weighted-polymorphism inequality
nodes.statement: Let $\phi\in\imp(W)$ be an $m$-ary weighted relation and let $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in D^m$ be such that $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in\dom(\phi)$. Since $\omega\in\wpol(\phi)$, we have, by~\eqref{eq:WPOL} with $\tup{x}_1=\tup{y}$ and $\tup{x}_i=\tup{x}$ for all $2\leq i\leq k$, and by~\eqref{eq:defNU}, $-\phi(\tup{y})-(k-1)\phi(\tup{x})+k\phi(\tup{x})\leq 0$, which gives $\phi(\tup{x})\leq\phi(\tup{y})$.
nodes.statement_short: Setting $\tup{x}_1=\tup{y}$ and the rest to $\tup{x}$ yields $\phi(\tup{x})\leq\phi(\tup{y})$.

nodes.name: Swap the tuples and conclude equality
nodes.statement: By swapping $\tup{x}$ and $\tup{y}$ in~\eqref{eq:WPOL}, we get $-\phi(\tup{x})-(k-1)\phi(\tup{y})+k\phi(\tup{y})\leq 0$, which gives $\phi(\tup{y})\leq\phi(\tup{x})$. Together, $\phi(\tup{x})=\phi(\tup{y})$ for all $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in\dom(\phi)$.
nodes.statement_short: The symmetric instantiation gives the reverse inequality, so $\phi$ is constant on $\dom(\phi)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 8
nodes.statement: Note that if $f$ is a minority operation then so is $g(x_1,x_2,x_3)=f(x_{\pi(1)},x_{\pi(2)},x_{\pi(3)})$ for any permutation $\pi$ on $\{1,2,3\}$. Thus, by Lemma~\ref{lem:perm}, we can assume $\omega$ assigns weight $-1$ to each of the three projections (and still every $f\in\supp(\omega)$ is a minority operation). Let $\phi\in\imp(W)$ be an $m$-ary weighted relation and let $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in D^m$ be such that $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in\dom(\phi)$. Since $\omega\in\wpol(\phi)$, we have, by~\eqref{eq:WPOL} with $\tup{x}_1=\tup{x}$ and $\tup{x}_2=\tup{x}_3=\tup{y}$, $-\phi(\tup{x})-2\phi(\tup{y})+3\phi(\tup{x})\leq 0$, which gives $\phi(\tup{x})\leq\phi(\tup{y})$. By swapping $\tup{x}$ and $\tup{y}$ in~\eqref{eq:WPOL}, we get $-\phi(\tup{y})-2\phi(\tup{x})+3\phi(\tup{y})\leq 0$, which gives $\phi(\tup{y})\leq\phi(\tup{x})$. Together, $\phi(\tup{x})=\phi(\tup{y})$ for all $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in\dom(\phi)$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the weighted-polymorphism inequality to $(\tup{x},\tup{y},\tup{y})$ and its swap to force $\phi(\tup{x})=\phi(\tup{y})$.

nodes.name: Normalise $\omega$ using Lemma 2
nodes.statement: Note that if $f$ is a minority operation then so is $g(x_1,x_2,x_3)=f(x_{\pi(1)},x_{\pi(2)},x_{\pi(3)})$ for any permutation $\pi$ on $\{1,2,3\}$. Thus, by Lemma~\ref{lem:perm}, we can assume $\omega$ assigns weight $-1$ to each of the three projections (and still every $f\in\supp(\omega)$ is a minority operation).
nodes.statement_short: Minority operations are permutation-closed, so Lemma 2 gives weight $-1$ on each of the three projections.

nodes.name: Instantiate the weighted-polymorphism inequality
nodes.statement: Let $\phi\in\imp(W)$ be an $m$-ary weighted relation and let $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in D^m$ be such that $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in\dom(\phi)$. Since $\omega\in\wpol(\phi)$, we have, by~\eqref{eq:WPOL} with $\tup{x}_1=\tup{x}$ and $\tup{x}_2=\tup{x}_3=\tup{y}$, $-\phi(\tup{x})-2\phi(\tup{y})+3\phi(\tup{x})\leq 0$, which gives $\phi(\tup{x})\leq\phi(\tup{y})$.
nodes.statement_short: With $\tup{x}_1=\tup{x}$, $\tup{x}_2=\tup{x}_3=\tup{y}$ the inequality gives $\phi(\tup{x})\leq\phi(\tup{y})$.

nodes.name: Swap the tuples and conclude equality
nodes.statement: By swapping $\tup{x}$ and $\tup{y}$ in~\eqref{eq:WPOL}, we get $-\phi(\tup{y})-2\phi(\tup{x})+3\phi(\tup{y})\leq 0$, which gives $\phi(\tup{y})\leq\phi(\tup{x})$. Together, $\phi(\tup{x})=\phi(\tup{y})$ for all $\tup{x},\tup{y}\in\dom(\phi)$.
